raw_comment:
I've noticed that most border crossings result in deportation orders or lengthy legal proceedings. Out of the 3.1 million migrants who crossed the southern border in 2023, 1.8 million are currently being processed. Approximately 58 percent of immigrants attempting to cross the southern border end up in legal trouble.  Furthermore, there were cases of deportation and expulsion, and an estimated 600,000 migrants entered undetected. With the upcoming presidential election, I'm wondering if  Trump wins will the number of migrants will decrease due to his political ideology, which favors harsher immigration policies. I also wonder if the number of undetected migrants entering this country will decrease under Trump's administration if he becomes President.  This graph relates to my community as many member in my town and school are immigrants. 

Title: The journey to America

raw_comment:
This graph illustrates all the border crossings in 2023 and that they resulted in three different processes. I noticed that none of the graphs resulted in citizenship however resulted in legal proceedings and legal limbo. I also noticed as the graph continued down into the path of acceptance to the United States the number of immigrants got smaller and smaller. I wonder how they estimated the number of undetected immigrants and if that is accurate. I also wonder why the expedited removal path goes into the legal proceedings path but then back out to the deported path. This relates to me and my community because I have many people in my community and in my personal life who have immigrated from the southern border. This graph helps me further understand the proceedings of immigration and how difficult it can really be. 
“Immigration investigation”

raw_comment:
I notice that 3.1 million people attempted cross the U.S.'s southern border in 2023. I notice that 600,000 immigrants entered undetected. I also noticed that 870,000 immigrants were deported, left voluntarily, or expelled from the U.S. Finally I notice that 1.8 million immigrants are still in legal limbo or in ongoing proceedings. This means that the majority of immigrants that attempted to enter the U.S. through our southern border in 2023 succeeded. I wonder why some immigrants are expelled under Title 42 and why some are processed under Title 8. I wonder how so many immigrants are able to enter the U.S. undetected. Clearly our border control cannot account for the millions of migrants attempting to immigrate to the U.S. I also what caused 180,000 migrants to leave voluntarily as this journey through or southern border is apparently very treacherous. I wonder if we will make progress in improving our border control and granting people citizenship in a more efficient way. This relates to myself and my community as the migrant crisis is a topic of conversation at my family dinner table as well as on the news frequently. This has been one of the topics in politics that I have been hearing about constantly for the past few years.

Migrant Mania

raw_comment: I initially noticed that almost all who attempted to cross were encountered by U.S Customs and Border Protection, with six hundred thousand entering undetected. This suggests the United States' high-security borders. About 2 million encountered were processed under Title 8, and only two thousand have gotten relief and are not in ongoing procedures. This may mean that the process is complex and lengthy. Of the 2.5 million encountered, a substantial number were expelled under Title 42. I wonder how 600-thousand were able to enter undetected, being that the border seemingly has a lot of control. Additionally, I wonder what the graph would look like if we could see the outcomes of those who entered undetectedly. I wonder how this graph looked in the past, and how it will look in upcoming years. This relates to me and my community, as it is important to recognize our country's border policies, given it is a controversial topic in the news very frequently. "Southern Border Struggles and Successes"

raw_comment:
This graph shows the attempted crossings at the U.S. southern border in 2023. In this graph, 1.8 million people who attempted to cross the border are in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo while 870,000 people have deportation orders, expulsion, etc. In addition, 600,000 immigrants entered undetected. Clearly, from this statistic, the border is not as secure as the government makes it seem as there is still a significant amount of people sneaking into this country illegally.  Title 42 says that when non-citizens enter the US on an illegal basis they will be processed for removal. Title 42 does not impose immigration or criminal consequences on migrants. Therefore, migrants who are expelled can repeatedly try and cross the border. I wonder how many migrants this past year attempted to cross the border for the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th time as a result of this law. I wonder how many of those migrants found undetected ways to enter. I also wonder why people would travel thousands of miles to this country and voluntarily depart once they begin being processed under Title 8. Is being processed really that bad? 180,000 people voluntarily departed once they began being processed under Title 8! This relates to me because my mom is an immigration lawyer and her job is to help people achieve immigration status in the United States. I am sure she is very familiar with all of this. 
"How Immigrants Make Their Way into the US"

raw_comment:
Most of the attempted US border crosses occur through border processes, such as under title 8, or through an exception such as under title 42, like during a pandemic or public health concern. Under title 8, most of the crossings occurred according to new immigration court cases. Also, an estimated fifth of the attempted US border crossings are undetected.

I wonder what the “relief granted” portion of title 8 crossings means. It is such a small fraction of the total US crossings, at only 2.7k, so I wonder how or why these occur.

This information could be important to educating not only immigrants, but citizens of the occurrences at the southern US border. Families whose success have depended upon entry to America can learn and know about such information, as well as people whose families have resided in the US for generations. It’s also interesting to me, as my dad is an immigrant who crossed the southern border.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all of the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: “For Migrants, Being Granted Relief in the U.S. Is Almost Impossible” by Ellie of Calif., “Operation Southern Border: Migrants vs Legal System” by Mia of Auburn, Wash., “What Happened to All of the People Who Attempted Crossing the U.S Border?" by Mia of Wilson Middle School in Chowchilla, Calif., “Crossing the Southern Border: The Odds of Success” of Katherine of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, N.J. and two headlines from Perth Amboy High School in N.J. -- “What's Next After Crossing the U.S Border?” by Karla and “How is America Dealing with Migrants on the Southern Border? by Alex.
 
Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that includes this graph.  Also in the Reveal are a summary of the topic, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph, and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.
 
The next graph will be released by Friday, March 1 with live-moderation on Wednesday, March 6.  The topic – Diet and Groundwater.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, whose grandparents entered the U.S. from New York City where the Statue of Liberty welcomed them, and David Wilcox of Lawrenceville, N.J., who believes that dreams span beyond borders.

raw_comment:
Out of 2.5 million encounters in this graph, 1.8 million immigrants are either still pending legal proceedings or are in legal limbo. Out of them, only 2,700 have been granted relief or residency, while 870,000 have been deported. 3.1 million people tried to cross the southern border into the United States in 2023; 1.8 million of them succeeded in doing so, 870,000 of them left the country, and about 602,700 were either ignored or granted amnesty.
Given that Title 42 was more permissive than Title 8 in permitting several attempts to cross the southern border, its termination raises concerns about the fate of undocumented immigrants and the length of their legal limbo. It's unclear how many unauthorized immigrants there are and how long they've been in legal limbo.
Perth Amboy, where I live and work and which attracts a lot of immigrants, worries about the ongoing immigration issues that its residents face. In an effort to provide for their families and become financially successful in the future, many immigrants, both first and second-generation, put a lot of effort into their employment. Disturbing statistics reveal that over 800,000 people were deported and only 2,700 people received aid, highlighting the ongoing struggles in the community.
How are Immigrants moving to the U.S. handled?

raw_comment:
This graph shows the statistics based on immigrants that cross over the American border in 2023. I notice that the number of immigrants expelled by Title 42 is quite large, and I wonder how that number will increase if President Biden expands the title, or how the number will decrease if he shrinks it. I also notice that only 2.7k immigrants have relief granted, which is shockingly low compared to the 2.5 million "Encounters" by U.S. Customs and Border Protection. I wonder how this number will grow or shrink as our society and government progresses. This affects me and my community because the immigrant crisis is a great one in America and I have a lot of empathy for struggling families trying to cross the border and it makes me very sad that it can be so hard for these families and individuals to come to America. 
"Immigration in America"

raw_comment:
This graph shows the attempts at crossing the U.S. Southern border in 2023. Almost 2.5 million out of 3.1 million were encountered by US customs and border protection. While the other 600k + came in undocumented. A lot of the 2.5 million who were encountered by customs were expelled and sent back to where they were coming from. I wonder what happened to all the pending cases. I also wonder how long the process is of becoming a citizen. This relates to me and my community because I am fortunate enough to be an American citizen and to live in this country. I also know people from my town who have immigrated from South America and are in the process of becoming a citizen.

raw_comment: The graph depicts how different people enter and interact with immigration in the United States. A large a number of people are made to leave under Title 42. raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

raw_comment: In this graph, it is displaying the different things that happened to migrants who attempted to cross the southern border in 2023. I noticed that there were 3.1 million attempts to cross the border, but only 600k entered undetected. I also noticed that the majority (1.8 million) of migrants were in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo compared to 870k facing deportation order, expulsion, etc. Additionally, I noticed that out of the people who faced deportation, order, expulsion, etc, the most (565k) were expelled under Title 42. I wonder what Title 42 and Title 8 are and why there are more people processed under Title 8 than expelled under Title 42. I also wonder why such little relief (2.7k) is granted to people. This relates to my community because I know many people who immigrated to the United States and I wonder if they had to face any of the processes that are listed in the graph. Also, I always hear about immigration issues in politics and know that it is presently a very highly debated topic. My headline for this graph would be: “Crossing the Border - A Not So Easy Process”.

raw_comment:
I notice that the majority of people who attempted crossing at the US southern border are in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo (1.8 million). I also notice that many of the people processed under Title 8 do not have an expedited removal or voluntary departure (365k). The most direction expulsion is through Title 42 (565k).

I wonder why so many individuals are in ongoing proceedings. Are they in jail during this time? I also wonder if other immigrants have similar rates of deportation. It would likely be more difficult to enter the US undetected if immigrating from overseas, but I am curious whether these individuals arrive in comparably extenuating circumstances.

This impacts my community because immigration affects the country's economy and atmosphere. Although I do not live in the South, policy on immigration still plays a role in elections. Furthermore, immigrants bring ideas and traditions from their home countries that contribute to our "melting pot."

The graph depicts the paths of immigrants attempting to cross the US southern border, showing the effects of legislation (Title 8 and Title 42) among other factors.

"Border Crossing Legislation Crosses the Line"

raw_comment:
What I notice is that 2.5 out of the 3.1 million attempted crossings at the U.S. southern border in 2023 were "Encounters" by U.S. Customs and Border protection. It is very interesting to see that they're not all just under one category per se but they can go under things such as Title 8 or could be considered "Non-border cases." Additionally, I noticed that it is truly difficult to try to cross the border undetected since so many were discovered or snuck in and were then deported. 

What I wonder is how people manage to keep track of all of these "cases" and if yes, how many are not included within the 3.1 million attempted crossings? Also what are the different ways immigrants manage to sneak in undetected by government officials or border patrol?

What's going on in this graph is it is trying to show the different ways each immigrant was either allowed, rejected, sent back after managing to enter the country, or so many other attempts at trying to start a different life for themselves. It is also emphasizing the amount of people who are truly trying to enter the country and want to leave the current one they are in. 

This relates to my community because there is a lot of politics surrounding immigration and I hear a lot of problems related to it within the news or how tons and tons of immigrants are sent primarily to New York City, which already is overpopulated, and the city is trying to manage the buses being sent their constantly.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? The graph shows what happens to migrants who attempt to cross the southern border of the United States of America. A good chunk of migrants are able to pass into America undocumented, while the majority encounter US forces. Of these approximated 2.5 million people who are processed by the US, another chunk is expelled or undergo other forms of deportations. However, the majority are put into the legal system and are in limbo, awaiting a court answer.
I wonder why so many people are in long-term legal limbo. Immigration from the southern border is such a big issue, so why hasn't the government allocated more resources to processing immigration cases? If the judicial process was easier, less people would feel the need to enter America undocumented. 
As someone who lives in America, I think that it's truly wrong that so many people who want to live here are hindered at every step by the government of the very place they want to live in. 
Headline: WHERE DO THEY GO? MIGRANTS IN AMERICA

raw_comment:
In this graph, I noticed the amount of migrants who attempted to cross the U.S. southern border in 2023 is a lot, approximately 3.1 million!! I notice that among these illegal migrants about 600,000 entered the US without detection. The process of becoming a US citizen is a tough one, which is why many desperate migrants feel the need to cross the southern border into the US illegally. The majority of immigrants who are not forced or choose to leave the United States are still in a place of uncertainty and a state of processing, about 1.8 million are still being processed. Immigration and the safety of the Southern border is a major topic in this present political climate. I wonder when the government is going to get its act together and fix its border protection laws. Recently, an illegal Venezuelan immigrant murdered a University of Georgia student and has a lengthy criminal record. This shows that the immigration process and the process of border protection need to be changed to prevent more killings of Americans. This affects me and my community because I am an American citizen, and I must be educated on this topic that is quite prevalent in politics today. 

Title: Crossing the Border Line

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that only 19% of those that enter the US southern border do so without being noticed. However, 81% are either relieved, deported, expelled, or in court. Depending on your political stance, this 19% figure may or may not be acceptable. I also notice that the estimated number of people who entered without being caught is 600,000. Finally, I see that title 8 is being used to process 1.9 million individuals. 

2) I wonder what Title 42 and how it was able to deport about 600,000 people in 2023 alone.  I also wonder how long it takes for migrants apprehended by border patrol to go through the legal system.

3) This is relevant to me and my community because, in an effort to improve their future, migrants are fleeing their past and creating an unprecedented border catastrophe. Additionally, as migrants cross the border, they settle in communities like New York where I am.

4) Journey For A Lifetime, It's All or Nothing for the Migrants vs USBP

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that most immigrants do not go undetected. I also notice that relief is only granted to a small amount of people that are processed under title 8. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder why some people have expedited removal but are also in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo. I wonder what title 8 and title 42 mean. I also wonder what happens later on to people who enter undetected. I wonder that of the people who are in legal limbo, how many are eventually granted relief or are deported.


How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because there in a huge influx of immigrants and I don’t believe there is enough space in states near the border for them to stay there so they may be moving to my community and surrounding areas. Near me in New York City, high school students were displaced from their school to make room for a place for immigrants to stay.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

raw_comment:
From the data, I noticed that the majority of migrants who attempted to cross the U.S. southern border were able to enter an ongoing proceedings or legal limbo. This is because out of the roughly 3.1 million migrants who crossed the southern border in 2023, 1.8 million are being processed. Another pathway in the process of crossing the border that occurred less frequently was deportation, expulsion and more. I also noticed that the number of migrants that “entered undetected” is estimated at 600,000. This is less accurate than the other documented data. I wonder how the statistics in the graph will change, if anything, in 2024? How will the 2024 presidential election impact the number of migrants in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo? Will the U.S. border security be tightened in the future to limit migrant crossings, or loosened? How do the amount of migrants who crossed the border impact the lives of other Americans? This graph relates to my community as migration and immigration are important topics that are discussed in the United States. With the 2024 presidential election coming up, Americans (including myself) have to decide how to vote concerning this topic. 

"The Migration Pathway in the U.S. Southern Border”

raw_comment:
I notice that most attempted crossings result in deportation orders, or long ongoing processes for legal immigration. 
This relates to my community because the people who are trying to enter the United States typically have a very good reason, one of which would be better opportunities and a better life. Since it is very difficult to successfully enter the US and become a legal citizen quickly, this will affect the population of people who strive for a better life in the US. 
I wonder why so many people decided to voluntarily depart, if they had already made it so far in the immigration process. 
"Crossing the Border: A Selective and Lengthy Process"

1) What do you notice? 
What I noticed about this graph is that there are different outcomes for those who attempt to cross the U.S. southern border in 2023. Approximately only about 1.8 million out of 3.1 million are in ongoing proceedings or legal limbos, with an estimated 600k entering the U.S. undetected.  
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder why 180k migrants decided to voluntarily depart if they were processed under Title 8, were the majority of these people frightened? 
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
The U.S. is a very diverse nation with several migrants entering the U.S. every day, communities are filled with people from different backgrounds and people get to view migrants achieving their hopes and dreams in a nation full of possibilities. 
4) What’s going on in this graph?
Would You Attempt To Cross The Border?

This graph showcases what happens to new immigrants who cross the border and the process they go through to possibly become citizens. It shows that around 3.1 million immigrants come through legally every year with around 600k sneaking in unnoticed. From the legal immigrants, a large amount eventually are deported and others make the process of becoming real citizens.

I wonder why so many immigrants get deported even after making it into the U.S. safely. For example, title 42 seems to be a large road bump for new immigrants

This impacts my community because as citizens of the U.S., we often hear about political issues about immigrants and it's important to understand what those issues mean and the path immigrants can legally make to become citizens. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

There are many bumps on the road to immigration

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that out of the 3.1 million immigrants who tried to cross the southern border during 2023. Approximately 600k of those did not get caught entering but, the rest have been put into different groups. I noticed how out of the 2.5 million immigrants who got caught 870k got deported, while there is 1.8 million in legal limbo. Lastly, I noticed how there were 2.7k people who were granted relief. 

2.  I wonder what are the considerations for each group. What considerations are being taken to be granted relief or to be under Title 8, or Title 42. As well as how those almost 600k immigrants were able to come in the country undetected.

3. This relates to and my community because many of my peers, and/or their families, as well as me  are immigrants and I know a few cases in which some of them have crossed the border and miserably failed.

4. Crossing Paths: The Southern Border Challenge?

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that there were about 3.1 million people attempting to cross the U.S. southern border in 2023 and only 1.8 million were able to be in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo. Also I noticed that crossing the border undetected is very hard, most migrants confront border control and then face legal hearings and others get deported. 
2. I wonder how this has changed over the years? For instance if more immigrants were able to come undetected or deported compared to past years?
3. This relates to me and my community because personally where I live there is a lot of hispanics and I know people who migrated to the United States, seeking for a better life, seeking better opportunities, and just in general seeking a better future. 
4. The Obstacles Faced by Immigrants on the Journey to the U.S.

Headline -> The Southern Gate; A way to hope or rejection.

I noticed that making through the border undetected is very rare in attempted crossings on the Southern border. Most migrants encounter border patrol and after that usually enter legal proceedings and legal battles to stay in the country.

raw_comment:
1) In this graph, 1.8 million immigrants remain in legal limbo or have continuing processes, out of 2.5 million interactions. Of these, 870,000 have been deported, with only 2,700 granted relief or residency. In 2023, 3.1 million persons attempted to enter the United States over the southern border, 1.8 million completed legal procedures, 870,000 returned to their home countries, and approximately 602,700 went unnoticed or awarded amnesty.

2) The end of Title 42 raises questions about the future of undocumented immigrants and the duration of their legal limbo, as it was lenient in allowing repeated attempts to cross the southern border, unlike Title 8. The estimated number of undocumented immigrants and their duration in legal limbo remains uncertain.

3) My community of Perth Amboy, an attraction for immigrants, is concerned about the persistent immigration challenges that its inhabitants encounter. Many first and second-generation immigrants work hard to improve the lives of their families in the hopes of achieving financial success in the future. The troubling data show that only 2,700 people received assistance, while over 800,000 were deported, demonstrating the community's continued hardships.

4)It’s Not as Easy as Just Crossing a Border: What’s Guaranteed for Future Immigration in America?

raw_comment:
I noticed that making through the border undetected is very rare in attempted crossings on the Southern border. Most migrants encounter border patrol and after that usually enter legal proceedings and legal battles to stay in the country. Meanwhile others are usually deported while only a small fraction get to actually stay in the country.

I wonder what Title 42 is and how it managed to deport almost 600k migrants in 2023 alone.  I also wonder how long the legal processes take when migrants are caught by border patrol.

This relates to me and my community as the border crisis is at an all time high as migrants attempt to escape their past in search for a better future. Also as migrants make it through the border they are settling in societies such as mine in Perth Amboy NJ.

Operation Southern Border: Migrants vs Legal System

- I notice that 1.8 million of the immigrants are in either legal limbo or in ongoing proceedings which is extremely high considering it is out of the population of 2.5 million of immigrants that have had "encounters". - I wonder how they estimated the amount of undocumented immigrants. Furthermore, for the figures on legal limbo I wonder how long these immigrants remain in proceedings or in legal limbo.

Which makes the figures shown in the graph extremely alarming with only 2,700 granted relief while over 800,000 were deported, demonstrating an extremely sad reality. 
- From Down And Under to the Land of the Free: To Stay or Likely Go

raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

On the other hand, 2.5 million migrants had "Encounters" with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, leading to deportation orders, expulsion, etc., or ongoing proceedings or legal limbo.

3) This relates to me and my community because many immigrants settled in Perth Amboy work hard to achieve a better life for their families, hoping that the next generations will excel and prosper in the future. 
4) One in a Million, Who Gets Past The U.S. Border?

raw_comment:
1) About 600k migrants have gotten across the southern border undetected. As you move down the graph, a chunk of people get deported; Title 42, voluntary departure, expedited removal. Even with the hundreds of thousands of deportations, millions of immigrants end up staying in the United States with only 2.7k having relief granted.
2) I wonder how a good portion of migrants were able to enter undetected. Is it because of coyotes (smugglers)? Why are there 180k migrants who choose to leave the country even after being processed under Title 8? How are there 1.8 million ongoing legal cases?
3) This relates to me and my community because I’m Mexican; I have plenty of family who have crossed the southern border. An aunt recently arrived in the States and it’s interesting to see that she could’ve been part of these data had she come a year earlier. It was through her that I learned what Title 42 is.
4) Life In The United States: To Be or Not To Be?

raw_comment:
I notice that most of the migrants have "encounters" by US Customs and Border Protection. From here there are many complicated legal processes that will either result in continued "legal limbo" or deportation.

I wonder why out of the 2.5 million migrants 870K are expelled and why 1.8 million people are involved in ongoing proceedings. What makes the final decision as to who gets expelled and who has continued debate on whether or not they can stay? I also wonder how we know 600K were able to enter undetected if the whole idea of undetected is that people didn't realize. How accurate is this figure?

This impacts our community because many families in states near ours are impacted by divided families due to the varying success of crossing the border. Some immigrants are still struggling with legal work, others get in undetected, and others are deported, potentially ripping apart families in the process.

A catchy headline for this graph could be "The 'Custom' Path of Entering the US"

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that only roughly 19% (600k/3.1m) of those that enter the US southern border do so without being noticed. However, 81% are either relieved, deported, expelled, or in court. Depending on your political stance, this 19% figure may or may not be acceptable. I also notice that the estimated number of people who entered without being caught is 600,000. Finally, I see that title 8 is being used to process 1.9 million individuals. 

2) I wonder what Title 42 and how it was able to deport about 600,000 people in 2023 alone.  I also wonder how long it takes for migrants apprehended by border patrol to go through the legal system.

3) This is relevant to me and my community because, in an effort to improve their future, migrants are fleeing their past and creating an unprecedented border catastrophe. Additionally, as migrants cross the border, they settle in communities like Perth Amboy, New Jersey, where I am.

4) Journey For A Lifetime, It's All or Nothing for the Migrants vs USBP

raw_comment:
1) Of the 3.1 million people who attempted to cross the border in 2023, only about 600,000 (or roughly around 19.4%) entered undetected. The rest were either deported (~28.1%) or processed (~61.3%). Of the 1.5 million people who underwent immigration court cases, very few were granted relief (around 0.18%).

2) I wonder why each immigration case is unique. How much does the ethnic background of a migrant affect what happens to them after attempting to cross the border?

3) This relates to me because I come from a family of immigrants and they crossed the southern border and experienced this themselves just to give us a better life. It's easy to forget that these numbers are actual people whose dreams are to carve a brighter future for their children. This also relates to my community because NJ is one of the states with the highest population of immigrants. 

4) The Border Experience

raw_comment:
What I notice is that approximately 600,000 people enter the country unnoticed, whereas the majority of attempted crossings at the U.S. border are met by legal patrol or border security (2.5 million). Five hundred sixty-six thousand were ejected under Title 42 and nine million were processed under Title 8 of the 2.5 million persons who came into contact with border patrol. 

This relates to me and my community because a lot of people where I live are predominantly Hispanic, therefore most kids in my school have Hispanic parents who may have experienced this or know someone that has.

In Or Out The Right Way The Choice Is Yours

raw_comment:
I noticed that making through the border undetected is very rare in attempted crossings on the Southern border. Most migrants encounter border patrol and after that usually enter legal proceedings and legal battles to stay in the country. Meanwhile others are usually deported while only a small fraction get to actually stay in the country.

I wonder what Title 42 is and how it managed to deport almost 600k migrants in 2023 alone.  I also wonder how long the legal processes take when migrants are caught by border patrol.

This relates to me and my community as the border crisis is at an all time high as migrants attempt to escape their past in search for a better future. Also as migrants make it through the border they are settling in societies such as mine in Perth Amboy NJ.

Operation Southern Border: Migrants vs USBP and the Legal System

Most attempted crossings at the U.S. border encountered legal patrol or Border protection (2.5 million), with only around 600k entering undetected. Out of the 2.5 million people who encountered border patrol, 1.9 million were processed under Title 8, and 565k were expelled under Title 42.

I am curious to know what determines if someone is processed under Title 8 rather than being expelled under Title 42. I would also like to know what they actually are and what they mean.

I think this impacts my community because there are many immigrants who come to the Portsmouth area and work here. Some are legal, but some are probably illegal as well.

Mapping Migration

raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

raw_comment: I notice that little less than 60% of those who attempt border crossings make it to a position where they could be accepted into the US. I also noticed that the estimated number of undetected crossings into the US is eerily similar to those expelled under Title 42 by US Customs or Border Protections. Only 2700 people out of the 1.5 million new-for-2023 immigration court cases receive relief and are allowed to stay in the US. In the tri-state area, we don’t necessarily take the brunt of the Southern border immigration flow. Yet we have the education to realize that wrong is happening at the border and in court for migrants at the Southern border, and we wish for change. I've always been frustrated by the way the Southern border has been handled and how those wishing to stay in the US are callously left in limbo by paperwork and trivialities. This graph shows just more of the same, which it should not. There needs to be changed, and I hope our generation can rise and make that change.

I noticed how the graph works top to bottom splitting up based on what happens to the immigrants. The thickness of each part shows how many immigrants there are, so the line for relief granted (2.7k) is the thinnest while the first one with 3.1 million is the thickest. The lines are color-coded, the yellow is ones who succeeded whether it was not getting caught or receiving legal aid, green was the ones who got caught and going through legal trouble, and purple is what happened to them, i.e getting deported, expelled, leaving on their own, etc. Only 19% of the estimated 3.1 million immigrants who crossed the border were able to make it through undetected and of the total 3.26 million between the border and non border cases only 18% were successful with either legal aid or being undetected and less than .1% succeeded legally with aid. 
2. 
How did they get the estimate of 600k undocumented crossings? How many of the 1.8 in legal limbo will get the legal aid that only 2.7k have gotten so far? Due to the large number of ones in legal trouble I wonder how long it takes.
3. 
We are far from the southern border so it does not have a large impact here locally. But it does impact the national community because there is a political divide over how to handle the immigrants.
4.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of people who cross the border into the United States and are detected by border patrol are either deported or have to deal with legal issues. A very small number of people are granted relief, about 2.7K according to the graph, compared to the 1.8 million people who are in ongoing legal proceedings or the 870K people who are deported. There is a larger amount of people who enter the United States through the southern border and stay, both detected and undetected, than the amount of people who enter the United States through the southern border and are expelled.
I wonder why out of all of the people who have been in immigration court cases, only a few of them have been granted relief. Only 2.7K people have been granted relief, while more than 600 times that are still dealing with legal proceedings.
This does not have a large impact on my community since I live in a small town in New Hampshire. New Hampshire is very far away from the southern border, so the majority of the issues that are happening in those states don’t affect us. Since I live in a small town, it is very unlikely that the people who cross the border will be moved here. The most it could affect me is hearing about the migrants being moved to the larger cities in New Hampshire, such as Nashua, Manchester, and Concord. I would hear people would talk about the news stories, but that would be the largest extent of effect to me.
What’s Actually Going On With the Migrants At the Border.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that about 80% of migrants are encountered by border control and legal action, whereas they estimate around 20% of migrants enter without being noticed. Also, about 80% of the migrants caught are then pushed into the court system under Title 8 which outlines how migrants should be handled at the border. The graph shows different paths that break off from each other and then lead to new outcomes, but all 2.5 million migrants found will ultimately be faced with a negative journey in the legal or deportation path. 
2. I wonder if this graph will push for any legislation to fix this overwhelming issue. I also wonder how this graph breaks down the section regarding processing under Title 8. What actions or decisions are given to migrants before extreme measures are taken? 
3. The problem of migrants coming over the border impacts my community in many ways. It causes an overwhelming amount of people to take over cities and communities. As these people are technically (though they should not be) illegal, they cannot find places to live, eat, or be employed. This can add to the homeless population of communities ultimately affecting how that community functions. However, I do not want to look at this problem as entirely negative because I do think migrants can add a lot to a community. They bring diversity through ideas, food, creativity, and more. 
4. “The impenetrable journey to crossing the U.S. southern border in 2023.”

raw_comment:
1. 3.1 million people attempted border crossings into U.S. territory. 600 thousand went undetected, 565 thousand were expelled under Title 42 (and later deported), and 2.5 million were processed under Title 8. Out of those 2.5 million, 185 thousand faced expedited removal and were later deported, 180 thousand voluntarily departed and were later deported, 1.5 million were added to court cases, and 300 thousand were paroled. As a remainder of the 2.5 million, 1.8 million are in ongoing proceedings or “legal limbo”.
	What I took away from this was that the majority of people immigrating into the U.S. are currently involved in court cases/legal limbo. Only 2.7 thousand people were let into the U.S, which was really surprising and sad to see, considering 3.1 million people tried to get into the U.S. which means roughly only 0.08% of people got into the U.S. legally.
2. How do they know that 600 thousand people made it undetected?
How do they know that this estimate is accurate?
3. For me, this doesn’t really have an impact on my community, since we aren’t that close to the Southern immigration flow. Because of this, I can't really speak from experience, but I will say that the way the borders have been handled lately, is just not good enough.

raw_comment:
I notice that little less than 60% of those who attempt border crossings make it to a position where they could be accepted into the US. I also notice that the estimated number of undetected crossings into the US is eerily similar to the number of those expelled under Title 42 by US Customs or Border Protections. Only 2700 people out of the 1.5 million new-for-2023 immigration court cases receive relief and are allowed to stay in the US.

I wonder why so few people (2.7k) eventually receive relief when the vast majority (1.8m) of people who are hoping to stay in the US are stuck in legal limbo or trying their best to make a case in an ongoing proceeding

In the tri-state area, we don’t necessarily take the brunt of the Southern border immigration flow. Yet we have the education to realize that wrong is happening at the border and in court for migrants at the Southern border, and we wish for change. I've always been frustrated by the way the Southern border has been handled and how those wishing to stay in the US are callously left in limbo by paperwork and trivialities. This graph shows just more of the same, which it should not. There needs to be change, and I hope our generation can rise and make that change.

The Quantified Flow of Southern Border Crossings.

raw_comment:
I notice that little less than 60% of those who attempt border crossings make it to a position where they could be accepted into the US. I also notice that the estimated number of undetected crossings into the US is eerily similar to the number of those expelled under Title 42 by US Customs or Border Protections. Only 2700 people out of the 1.5 million new-for-2023 immigration court cases receive relief and are allowed to stay in the US.

I wonder why so few people (2.7k) eventually receive relief when the vast majority (1.8m) of people who are hoping to stay in the US are stuck in legal limbo or trying their best to make a case in an ongoing proceeding

In the tri-state area, we don’t necessarily take the brunt of the Southern border immigration flow. Yet we have the education to realize that wrong is happening at the border and in court for migrants at the Southern border, and we wish for change. I've always been frustrated by the way the Southern border has been handled and how those wishing to stay in the US are callously left in limbo by paperwork and trivialities. This graph shows just more of the same, which it should not. There needs to be change, and I hope our generation can rise and make that change.

The Quantified Flow of Southern Border Crossings.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the majority of people that attempted to cross into the US Southern border in 2023 were now in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo. It was interesting to note the amount of people that entered and were undetected, around a 600k estimate. It was interesting to see that there were two titles that the people were evaluated under, Title 8 and Title 42, but with Title 42, 565k were deported.
2. After looking at the graph I have questions about what the Title 8 and Title 42 are specifically about. What sorts of things do they look at and what factors determine how they are used? How big of a role does Title 42 and Title 8 play in this process?
3. It is eye opening to see the process that those who cross the Southern border have to go through. There are so many different things that could happen and factors that could impact their future just in this process alone. It is disheartening to see that only 2.7k out of the 3.1 million people that attempted to cross the border received relief. I would say that the attempted crossings at the Southern border do not have as large of an impact on my community which is closer to the northern US borders. 
4. Cross or Not? US Southern Border in 2023

raw_comment: Of the 3.1 million attempted crossings at the southern border, 600,000 are estimated to have entered and remain undetected, while 2.5 million are “caught” by customs and border protection. I thought it was a little disturbing that only 2,700 were allowed relief legally while 870,000 were expelled or deported from the country. I wonder where these people go after they are removed from the country and what their futures hold for them after trying to come to America. I think our communities would be much better served having more help for immigrants when they are here whether legally or illegally and for everyone struggling to have a stable life of their own. The title I came up with for the graph was "0.08% Chance of Relief".

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
The majority of migrants do not end up in a state of resolutions, but are caught up in “legal limbo” or ongoing cases. The next largest group is deported or expelled, while only a tiny fraction of the people (less than 0.1%) are granted relief legally. The only realistic way for them to enter the country is to do so undetected, which an estimated 600k do, since an encounter with customs all but guarantees rejection or an indeterminate result.

2. What do you wonder?

What does deportation/expulsion look like? Is there a specific protocol for bringing them back, or do they just get told to walk in the other direction? Also, what differentiates those granted relief from the vast majority who are not? Is there a special criteria they must meet? Lastly, what are “non-border cases”, and how do they enter the picture?

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
I’m not sure that there are many migrants who arrive in my local area, but this certainly has an impact on my larger, national community. The large number of migrants can have an impact on cities that they arrive in. In some cases, this means filling jobs which are unwanted by other parts of the population, or in some cases by putting a stress on welfare systems. It also has an impact on politics, since immigration issues can polarize people’s views.


4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Legal Limbo: The Fate of People Entering America

4. 'The Impossible Loop of Immigration into the U.S.'

raw_comment:
1. My eyes were first drawn to the complexity of the graphic which could be indicative of the complexity of seeking asylum and safety in the United States. As my eyes wandered around the graphic I noticed that the vast majority of migrants get deported whether immediately or eventually but most usually get deported after long and expensive legal battles with our country’s judicial system. I finally made it to the bottom of the graphic and saw that out of 3.1 million asylum seekers who enter our country each year, only 2.7 thousand are granted asylum and relief but only after a long journey from the desert to the courts that can take up to a decade to wrap up. 

2. It makes me wonder how much time, resources, and money would be saved if we provided migrants with an easy and accessible path to citizenship.

3. The influx of undocumented people into our cities causes issues with sustainable houses, clothing, and food, especially in the winter. Unfortunately, undocumented people are not granted the same courtesy that US citizens and permanent residents are granted in terms of rights, jobs, and resources. As a US permanent resident, I understand the complexities and intricacies of gaining US citizenship and navigating through immigration courts and I will always advocate for the recognition and naturalization of undocumented people in the US.

4. A Journey to Futility: Crossing the US Southern Border

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice many things about this graph. One striking statistic is that only 2,700 immigrants, out of the 3.1 million person total, become legal citizens of the United States (0.08%). Additionally, 185k immigrants are forced into expedited removal which the National Immigration Forum describes as deportation in as little as one day without a hearing. Interestingly, about 58% of cases result in proceedings or “legal limbo”. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how are expedited removals and deportations carried out. Are the immigrants literally put on planes or vans back into their home countries? How is the total of undocumented immigrants calculated? Why do some choose voluntary departure? Lastly, how does the US court system determine who is eligible or who should deserve relief? How can we help process immigration cases faster and help immigrants access better opportunities?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The government needs some way to pay for all of the resources needed to deal with this issue. This money comes from US taxes. This can affect many communities with an influx of immigrants, documented or not. This topic of a great increase in immigration does not majorly impact where I am from as I do not live close to the border or any major cities. 
4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
The Southern Border Byproduct: What is Really Happening With Illegal Immigration?

raw_comment:
1.
I noticed ⅕ that the migrants entered the US without being detected. Out of the 3.1 million who have entered the US through the southern border, 2.5 million encountered U.S. customs and border protection. The result of this was that 1.5 million more court cases were added this year after being processed under Title 8. 
2.
I wonder why there are no new laws enforced or made to stop or reduce the amount of migrants entering undetected. I wonder if this number will continue to grow and how much more will need to enter in order for there to be change. Titles 8 and 42 were presented on the data. I also wonder what determines a person to be under either 8 or 42. 
3.
These migrants who are entering the U.S. need a place to go. Whether it's planned for where they are going or unplanned, they are traveling throughout the U.S., most with the idea of getting away from the Southern borders as much as possible, thus moving north. This can impact our community greatly if we start to receive migrants at an increasing rate. Jobs will be harder to get, prices could increase, and more living space and conditions will be at stake. Currently, we don’t see a lot of this in New England because it's such an expensive place to live. 
4.
2023 in Review of Migrants Crossing the Southern Boarder.

2. I wonder why the U.S. takes in so few immigrants.  Why are our immigration quotas so low compared to other first-world countries?  Why is a country built from immigrants letting in so few immigrants?

Less immigrants means less experience with the outside world, so we are quite a sheltered community.  Our community could easily support immigrants as well, because it is quite affluent.
4. "The odds are against migrants"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
With this graph, I notice that as the graph decreases, more immigrants are either caught or taken into account by United States Law Enforcement. Around 600,000 people entered the country undetected, which seems like a very high number, as that is almost 20% of all immigrants. Only .1% receive legal relief. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what “expelled under 42” implies and how the United States would go about sending those caught back to their native country. What does title 8 mean in comparison to title 48? I wonder how almost 3,000 immigrants are granted relief, and what exactly that entails. 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impact that this directly has on me is very small, as I’m thousands of miles away from the Southern Border. But this impact does affect me morally, as it’s always unfortunate to hear what’s happening on the southern border, and it entails to me as a United States citizen. 
4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
The Improbable Success Rate of Crossing the Southern Border

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that there are a total of 3.1 million people who try to cross the southern border every year and only 2.7k  have relief granted. The likelihood of getting relief granted is around 0.08% likelihood of getting what they came for. I also noticed that around 600k people entered undocumented into the US. Overall I notice that the immigration system into the US might not be the most efficient. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what caused the system to be so inefficient as 200k people could have left because they were sick of waiting. I also wonder how other countries' immigration processes are maybe just as inefficient or maybe one country has a very effective process. 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
One impact that this has on our community is that it makes us aware of problems that we don’t face. In the northeast we don’t have many immigrants coming here but if we had an influx of 1.8 million that would mean double New Hampshire's population. That would be very difficult for the Northeast to do as we can see in what happened in New York City recently.
4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Less than a 0.08 percent chance of getting through, Legally

raw_comment:
The majority of people immigrating into the USA are still involved with a court case. Only 2.7k people were able to get into the country. 
I wonder why so few are able to get into this country. I find it hard to believe that out of 3.1 million people, only 2.7k were able to legally get into the country.
This relates to me and my community because I advocate extensively for workers rights, and the people who suffer the most from a lack of these are immigrant workers. They are not offered the same protections as naturalized US citizens. This is an easy way to lock somebody into a job that does not adhere to the law (under the threat of deportation). Many people say immigrants bring guns and drugs into the country, yet more often than not, it is business owners and capitalists profiting off of illegal labour.
The USA used to be seen as a country of economic opportunity, nowadays, it is a trap of cheaper, demeaning, and unsafe labour.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the biggest endpoint category for migrants is “in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo”. Relief was only granted for the tiniest amount of people, 2700. I also noticed that there were two Titles, Title 8 and Title 42, that could impact what happened to the person. With Title 8, the migrants were “processed,” but with Title 42, there were immediately “expelled”
2. I wonder what Title 8 and Title 42 are, and what determines which one is used for a particular person. I also wonder if this chart would look any different for people who entered the country a different way, such as crossing the northern border.
3. The fact that almost all of the migrants aren’t granted relief gives a lot of perspective because that’s almost 3 million people who were either turned away or are still trying to make it happen. 
4. It’s a Lottery: For Migrants, Being Granted Relief in the U.S. is Almost Impossible

raw_comment:
I notice that the combination of the approximate amount of immigrants who entered undetected or were given relief (602,700) was less than the total immigrants who were denied access or voluntarily departed (930k). Out of the whole, about  1,567,300 immigrants are in legal limbo, which is about 50.6% of the whole. 

I wonder why there is no new legislation passed to regulate the border cases. I know that there is intense political gridlock on this very polarizing issue, however the more time migrants spend at the border, the more money the government is spending anyways. If the government were to create better legal infrastructure, and yes, spend more money now to create it, the process might be expedited and cause less distress for the government and the migrants. 

I am a child of two immigrants who emigrated to the US legally. However, it has become increasingly difficult to emigrate to the US because of the practices at the border and seemingly never-ending paperwork, put in place to make the process drawn out. I do believe that there needs to be a better vetting system of candidates, in both that dangerous people are not let into the US, but also that people who deserve legal entry are granted this. There has long been abuse of migrant labor through H1 and green cards, but the malpractice at the border and abuse of migrants saddens me, especially when a key pillar of American government is equality of opportunity.  

Give US your tired & poor; but only if you're a citizen

What do you notice?
- Of the immigrants that entered the United States, almost the same number were expelled under Title 42. On the contrary, of the 1.9 million that were processed under Title 9, 1.8 million have ongoing legal procedures. It is important to note that of the 1.8 million with ongoing legal trials, 180k are non-border related.

What do you wonder?
-I wonder why there is roughly the same number of those who entered undetected as those who were expelled under Title 42. Also, why do they include the 180k of non-related border cases in the 1.8 million court dealings?

- 2023 Overview of Immigration into the United States through the Southern Border
